Arthur and Elaine Aron's self-expansion model (1986) helps explain why. We are attracted to people who widen us, and a partner who keeps growing in their own direction keeps bringing new territory home. Fully merged, there is nothing left to discover. The poets knew it first. Rilke, in his seventh letter to the young poet Franz Kappus (1904), described a love in which two solitudes protect, border and greet each other. Kahlil Gibran's The Prophet (1923) asks lovers to let there be spaces in their togetherness, like the strings of a lute, which are alone though they quiver with the same music. Distance here is not coldness or a game of withdrawal. It is the air between two fires, without which neither burns.

tales.title: The Lamp and the Wing
tales.who: Psyche and Cupid (Eros)
tales.when: myth, written down c. AD 160 to 180
tales.where: an enchanted palace in an unnamed kingdom
tales.source: Apuleius, Metamorphoses (The Golden Ass), books IV to VI
tales.tale:
Apuleius gives the story to an old woman in a robbers' cave, who tells it to comfort a kidnapped bride, and it still has the feel of a fairy tale whispered in the dark. A king has three daughters, and the youngest, Psyche, is so beautiful that people abandon the temples of Venus to stare at her instead. The goddess, insulted, sends her son Cupid to make the girl love some wretched creature. Cupid looks at Psyche and falls himself.

An oracle orders her family to leave her on a mountain crag, dressed as if for her funeral, to wed a winged monster. Instead the west wind lifts her gently down into a valley, to a palace of gold and citron wood where invisible voices draw her bath and unseen hands play the lyre at supper. Her husband comes only after dark. She hears his voice, feels his body, never sees his face, and he asks only this: do not try to see me.

For a while it is enough. The not-seeing is its own heat; every night is an arrival. But her sisters visit, envious of the palace, and they plant a seed: what if he is a serpent fattening you for the kill? One night Psyche hides a lamp and a razor. When he sleeps she lifts the light, and there on her pillow lies the most beautiful of the gods, his wings soft with feathers, a bow and quiver at the foot of the bed. She touches an arrow, pricks her thumb, and falls in love with Love himself. Leaning closer, she lets a drop of hot oil fall on his shoulder. He wakes, sees the lamp, and flies.

What follows is her long apprenticeship in distance. Venus sets her impossible tasks: a heap of mixed grains to sort by nightfall, golden wool from murderous sheep, water from the source of the Styx, a box of beauty fetched from Proserpina in the underworld. Psyche, alone, accomplishes them, helped by ants, a whispering reed, an eagle. At the last she opens the box and sinks into a deathlike sleep. Cupid, healed and longing, finds her, wipes the sleep from her eyes and wakes her with a harmless prick of his arrow. Jupiter makes her immortal, and their daughter is named Voluptas: Pleasure.
tales.reveals: Desire burned brightest while Psyche could not fully possess her lover, and it was lost the moment she tried to pin him down under a lamp. Love was won back only through separation, once she had become someone in her own right. The myth suggests that total possession kills what longing keeps alive, and that two people must each make their own journey to meet as equals.

tales.title: Two Houses and a Bridge
tales.who: Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera
tales.source: the twin house-studios designed by Juan O'Gorman (1931 to 1932), now the Museo Casa Estudio Diego Rivera y Frida Kahlo; Kahlo's diary; Hayden Herrera, Frida (1983)
tales.tale:
In 1931 the young architect Juan O'Gorman drew something unusual for Diego Rivera: not one house but two. On a corner lot in San Ángel, behind a fence of living organ cactus, rose a large studio painted rose-red with a saw-toothed roof to catch the north light, and beside it a smaller cube painted a blue as hard as the Mexican sky. The big one was for Diego, the small one for Frida. A narrow bridge ran between their roof terraces, high above the garden.

They moved in when they came back from the United States in 1934. He was forty-seven, enormous, famous, surrounded by assistants, models, visitors, pre-Hispanic idols and the constant noise of commissions. She was not yet twenty-seven, small, fierce, still thought of by many as the great man's wife who also painted. In her own house she had her own easel, her own bed, her own door. She could cross to him by the bridge. She could also not cross.

This is no tidy fable of healthy boundaries. The San Ángel years were among the most painful of their life together. Diego began an affair with Frida's younger sister Cristina, and Frida answered with A Few Small Nips (1935), a painting of a woman stabbed on a bed by a man who shrugs. She took lovers of her own, among them the sculptor Isamu Noguchi. In 1939 they divorced.

And yet the separate houses did something the marriage alone could not. In her blue cube Frida became a painter the world could not ignore: André Breton championed her, the Louvre acquired one of her pictures, and Diego, who never lied about painting, praised her work above his own. He watched her across the rooftop not only as a wife but as an artist, a stranger he kept having to discover. A year after the divorce, on 8 December 1940, his fifty-fourth birthday, they married again in San Francisco.

In her late diary she wrote his name down the page like a litany: Diego beginning, Diego builder, Diego my child, Diego my lover, Diego my husband, Diego my friend, Diego equals me. The houses had given each of them a room. The bridge had given them a reason to cross.
tales.reveals: Two artists with enormous appetites kept their desire alive by keeping separate worlds that faced each other. The distance did not prevent wounds, and it is no cure for betrayal, but it let each become someone the other had to keep rediscovering. A bridge only means something when there are two sides.

practice: Keep one pursuit this week that is entirely yours (a class, a long run, a project), and let your partner hear about it afterwards rather than watch it happen.
Arrange to see her in her element, at work, among friends, doing something she is good at, and look at her the way a stranger at the party would.
Spend an evening apart on purpose, then meet somewhere new as if for a first date, each with something to tell.
Notice the urge to know everything (her phone, her every hour) and leave it unsatisfied: let some of her life stay her own.
principles.shadow: Distance turns cruel when it is used to punish, to keep someone anxious, or to hide a second life. Space you take should be spoken of openly and should always lead back toward the other.

principles.title: Speak to every sense
principles.motto: The mind can be argued with; the senses simply believe.
principles.essence: Attraction is not only a meeting of minds but of bodies in a room: a voice, a scent, a texture, a taste, the quality of the light. Become someone whose presence is a pleasure to every sense, and learn to read the other's senses as carefully as her words.
principles.depth: Smell is the oldest of the senses and the most direct. Olfactory signals reach the amygdala and hippocampus, centres of emotion and memory, through fewer relays than sight or sound, which is why, as Rachel Herz has shown in studies since the 1990s, memories evoked by scent feel more emotional than those triggered by pictures. Claus Wedekind's famous T-shirt study (1995) suggested that women preferred the smell of men whose immune genes differed from their own; later work has been mixed, so treat it as a tantalizing hint rather than a law. Touch has its own channel: Löken and colleagues (2009) described nerve fibres, C-tactile afferents, that respond best to slow stroking at roughly the speed of a caress and carry feeling rather than information. Harry Harlow's infant monkeys (1958), clinging to a soft cloth mother rather than a wire one that gave milk, showed how deep the need runs. Literature knew all this. Proust raised a cathedral of memory on a crumb of madeleine dipped in lime-blossom tea (Swann's Way, 1913). Merleau-Ponty argued in Phenomenology of Perception (1945) that we do not merely have bodies but are them, and know the world through them. A seduction that addresses only the intellect is speaking to one guest at a crowded table.

tales.title: A Garden Locked, a Garden Opened
tales.who: the Shulammite woman and her beloved
tales.when: compiled perhaps 5th to 3rd century BC from older love songs (dating debated)
tales.where: ancient Israel: Jerusalem, Lebanon and the vineyards of En-gedi, in the poem
tales.source: The Song of Songs (Song of Solomon), quoted from the King James Version (1611); Rabbi Akiva's verdict in the Mishnah, Yadayim 3:5
tales.tale:
It begins mid-kiss, without preamble. “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth: for thy love is better than wine.” No narrator introduces the speakers, no prophet frames the scene, and God is not named once in its eight short chapters. Yet it sits in the Bible, and when the rabbis debated whether it belonged there, Rabbi Akiva answered that all the scriptures are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies.

It is a poem made almost entirely of senses. The woman speaks first and most often. She is darkened by the sun from keeping her brothers' vineyards, and unashamed of it: “I am black, but comely.” Her lover is “a bundle of myrrh” lying between her breasts, “a cluster of camphire in the vineyards of En-gedi.” Faint with longing, she asks to be revived with raisin cakes and fruit: “stay me with flagons, comfort me with apples: for I am sick of love.” He answers with a catalogue of praise: lips like a thread of scarlet, temples like a split pomegranate behind her veil, hair like a flock of goats streaming down Mount Gilead, the scent of Lebanon in her garments.

Then he calls her “a garden inclosed,” a spring shut up, a fountain sealed, full of spikenard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon. And she, not he, answers: “Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out. Let my beloved come into his garden.” The opening is hers to give.

The finest scene happens at night. She lies half asleep: “I sleep, but my heart waketh.” He knocks, his hair wet with dew. She hesitates; she has already undressed and washed her feet. He puts his hand through the latch-hole, and her whole body stirs. She rises to open, and her fingers drip with sweet myrrh onto the handles of the lock. But when the door swings back, he is gone. She runs through the dark streets calling him, and the watchmen find her and strike her.

The poem never resolves into a wedding or a moral. It ends with a seal set upon the heart, with the claim that love is strong as death and that many waters cannot quench it, and with a last call to make haste, like a young stag upon the mountains of spices.
tales.reveals: The Song treats desire as a feast for every sense, braiding scent, taste, touch, sound and sight until the body becomes a landscape. It gives the woman the first word and the opening of the garden, and lets longing include missed chances and pursuit. Its sensuality is reverent, mutual and astonishingly specific.

tales.title: The Sixty-Four Arts
tales.who: Vatsyayana Mallanaga and the nagaraka, the cultivated city-dweller of his text
tales.where: northern India, in the idealized household the text describes
tales.source: Vatsyayana, Kama Sutra, Book 1 (chapters 3 and 4) and Book 2 (chapter 10); translation by Wendy Doniger and Sudhir Kakar (2002)
tales.tale:
Ask most people what the Kama Sutra is and they will describe a manual of positions. The Victorian translation of 1883 by Richard Burton and Forster Fitzgerald Arbuthnot, printed for private circulation, did much to fix that image. But open the book itself, composed in Sanskrit by a scholar named Vatsyayana, probably in the third century, and the first thing you meet is a curriculum.

Before any embrace, Vatsyayana lists sixty-four arts that a cultivated person, woman as well as man, should learn. They include singing, playing instruments and dancing; painting, and laying patterns of flowers on the floor and on the bed; making garlands and head ornaments; mixing perfumes and preparing drinks; playing music on glasses filled with water; teaching parrots and mynah birds to talk; solving riddles, capping verses, knowing other languages and the dialects of distant regions; carpentry, conjuring tricks, games of dice. A courtesan who masters them, he says, earns a seat of honour in any gathering, and a woman who knows them can support herself even far from home.

Then he paints a room. The nagaraka, the man about town, lives in a house near water, with a garden. His bedroom holds a soft bed white with clean sheets, a smaller couch, a stand with perfumes and fragrant pastes, a box of betel. On an ivory peg hangs a lute. There is a board for drawing, a box of colours, a book, garlands of amaranth; caged birds hang outside. In the morning he bathes, perfumes himself, reddens his lips with lac, studies his face in a mirror and chews betel to sweeten his breath. Afternoons are for talk, poetry and games; evenings for music, and for the guest he has been expecting.

And afterwards, the text insists, lovers should not simply part. They climb to the roof terrace to enjoy the moonlight. She lies in his lap, facing the sky, and he points out the stars to her: the Pole Star, faithful Arundhati, the Seven Sages. They eat sweet things, drink fresh juice and talk tenderly.

It is the opposite of a mechanical handbook. Vatsyayana's ideal lover is a host of all the senses, whose music, scent, conversation, food and starlight come before and after the body and give it meaning.
tales.reveals: In the oldest surviving Indian treatise on desire, the bed is only one chapter: the real art is to make every sense a source of pleasure and every meeting a whole evening. Sensuality, for Vatsyayana, was a discipline of culture and attention open to women as well as men, and it ended not in departure but in shared wonder under the stars.

practice: Choose one scent that becomes yours and wear it lightly and consistently, so that in time it starts to mean you.
Listen to your own voice this week: slow it down, lower the volume at the moments that matter, and let pauses do some of the work.
Plan one evening for every sense: a lamp instead of overhead light, music chosen in advance, something good to taste, a fabric that feels lovely, and no screens.
Study her senses too: what she touches when she is nervous, which song changes her face, which food makes her light up. Remember it, and bring it back later.
principles.shadow: Sensuality becomes manipulation when it is used to overwhelm someone's judgment, with alcohol, pressure or a setting designed to make saying no awkward. Pleasure offered should leave the other freer, never foggier.

principles.title: Play, masks and fantasy
principles.motto: Behind a mask, people dare to be who they secretly are.
principles.essence: A love that only ever happens as itself grows narrow. Invite imagination in: roles, games, disguises, invented worlds, private stories only the two of you share. Play lets each of you be more than one person, and lets desire travel where ordinary life never goes.
principles.depth: Johan Huizinga, in Homo Ludens (1938), described play as stepping into a magic circle: a space set apart, with its own rules, where ordinary consequences are suspended and people try on other selves. D. W. Winnicott, in Playing and Reality (1971), went further, arguing that it is only in playing that a child or an adult is able to be fully creative, and only in being creative that a person discovers the self. Oscar Wilde compressed it into a paradox in The Critic as Artist (1891): man is least himself when he talks in his own person; give him a mask, and he will tell you the truth. Psychology supports the instinct. Reviewing decades of research, Harold Leitenberg and Kris Henning (1995) found sexual fantasy to be nearly universal among adults and, for most people, associated with healthy rather than troubled sexuality. Arthur Aron and colleagues (2000) found that couples who shared novel, mildly challenging activities reported greater relationship satisfaction than couples who shared merely pleasant, familiar ones. Mikhail Bakhtin saw the medieval carnival as a temporary world turned upside down, where hierarchies loosened and the body laughed. Lovers can build small carnivals of their own: worlds for two, entered by agreement and left at will.

tales.title: The Nun in the Mask
tales.who: Giacomo Casanova and the nun he calls M.M.
tales.where: Venice, and the convent of Santa Maria degli Angeli on Murano
tales.source: Giacomo Casanova, Histoire de ma vie (written 1789 to 1798), the Venetian chapters; his account is unverifiable in many details, and M.M.'s identity is disputed (one proposal is Marina Maria Morosini)
tales.tale:
Casanova wrote his memoirs as an old man, exiled in a Bohemian castle, and he is not a reliable witness. But few chapters are as strange or as theatrical as his account of M.M.

In the autumn of 1753 he was twenty-eight, back in Venice, and attending Mass at a convent on the island of Murano, where a girl he loved had been placed by her father. One day, he says, a letter reached him from another nun of that convent. She had noticed him in church; she proposed to meet him, first in the convent parlour, behind its iron grille, and then elsewhere. She was young, educated, a freethinker, and beautiful in a way her habit could not hide.

The rendezvous was set for an hour after sunset, at the foot of the bronze horseman of the condottiere Colleoni beside the church of Santi Giovanni e Paolo. Casanova waited in the dark square. A figure in men's clothes and a mask crossed the stones toward him, and only when she spoke did he know her. She led him by gondola to a casino, a small and elegant apartment she kept with the help of a rich protector: mirrors, porcelain, little suppers, books he never expected a nun to own.

This was the Venice of carnival, when for months of the year almost anyone could walk the city in the white bauta mask and black tabarro cloak, and a patrician and a fishmonger could not be told apart. M.M. used it as a stage. As he tells it, she slipped out of the convent by water at night, traded her habit for silk or a man's coat, and was back inside before the bells. She wrote him long, witty letters and devised games, suppers and surprises; once she sent to the casino, in her place, the very girl he had first loved in that convent.

There was a darker theatre too. Her protector was the French ambassador, the Abbé de Bernis, and Casanova later learned that Bernis had watched them from a hidden cabinet. He records it with an arch shrug; a modern reader may not. The affair ended in July 1755, when the State Inquisitors arrested Casanova and locked him under the lead roof of the Doge's Palace. Forty years later, he was still writing about her.
tales.reveals: Masks, cross-dressing, stolen hours and a theatre of letters turned an affair into a shared work of imagination, and Casanova remembered it to the end of his life. The tale also shows where play turns murky: once a hidden third party watches, the game is no longer one everyone has chosen. Fantasy is magnetic precisely because it is agreed.

tales.title: Woo Me, I Am in a Holiday Humour
tales.who: Rosalind (disguised as Ganymede) and Orlando
tales.when: written c. 1599; set in a timeless pastoral
tales.source: William Shakespeare, As You Like It, acts 3 to 5 (fiction)
tales.tale:
Rosalind is banished from her uncle's court with almost nothing, and she does what clever heroines do: she disguises herself. Being, as she says, more than common tall, she puts on doublet and hose, hangs a boar-spear at her side and calls herself Ganymede, after Jove's own page. Her cousin Celia becomes the shepherdess Aliena, and the two of them, with the court fool Touchstone, walk into the Forest of Arden.

There she finds bad love poetry hanging on the trees. “From the east to western Ind, / No jewel is like Rosalind.” The poet is Orlando, the young man she fell for at a wrestling match, now also exiled, also in Arden, carving her name into the bark like a lovesick schoolboy.

A lesser play would have her throw off the disguise at once. Rosalind does something more daring. Still dressed as Ganymede, she tells Orlando she can cure him of love. He must come to her cottage every day, call her Rosalind, and woo her. She will play his lady, moody, changeable, impossible, until he is sick of the whole business.

So the courtship becomes a game within a game. Orlando arrives an hour late, and she scolds him: a lover who breaks a promise by a fraction of a minute may have been clapped on the shoulder by Cupid, but his heart is whole. She mocks his clichés. When he swears he will die if Rosalind refuses him, she punctures it: “Men have died from time to time, and worms have eaten them, but not for love.” And then, in the very act of mocking love, she gives herself away: “Come, woo me, woo me, for now I am in a holiday humour, and like enough to consent.” She has Celia marry them in jest, and the joke trembles with the real thing.

Under the mask Rosalind can say what no well-bred young woman at court could say: what she wants, what she fears, how men and women actually behave. She tests Orlando, educates him, and falls deeper herself. On Shakespeare's stage a boy actor played her, a boy playing a woman playing a man playing a woman, and the audience savoured every layer. When she finally reveals herself, the forest bursts into four weddings. Orlando had confessed the day before that he could live no longer by thinking. The game had made the real thing possible.
tales.reveals: The disguise freed Rosalind to be wittier, bolder and more honest than her station allowed, and it let Orlando court a person rather than an ideal. Play built a safe stage on which both could rehearse love before risking it. The mask did not hide the truth; it let the truth out.

practice: Propose a small game with a clear frame: meet at a bar as if you were strangers, and stay in character for the first half hour.
Build a private world: a nickname, an invented ritual, a running story that only the two of you continue.
Share one daydream you have never acted on, then ask, gently and without pressure, about one of hers; listen without judging.
Agree on a simple word that ends any game instantly, and honour it without sulking: safety is what makes boldness possible.
principles.shadow: Fantasy goes wrong when the mask is used to deceive someone about who you really are, or when a role is imposed rather than chosen. Every game needs the consent of everyone in it, including anyone watching, and an exit that works.

principles.title: The dance of power and surrender
principles.motto: Desire sparks where two strengths meet and take turns yielding.
principles.essence: Attraction often lives in a charge between opposites: leading and following, holding firm and letting go. The art is not to dominate or to disappear, but to be strong enough to lead and secure enough to surrender, and to let those roles pass back and forth between you.
principles.depth: The interpersonal circumplex, which grew out of Timothy Leary's work in the 1950s and was refined by Donald Kiesler and others, maps behaviour on two axes, warmth and dominance, and predicts complementarity: warmth invites warmth, but dominance tends to invite deference, and deference invites leadership. Larissa Tiedens and Alison Fragale (2003) tested this with posture. When a partner sprawled expansively, participants who drew themselves in felt more comfortable and liked that partner more than those who mirrored the pose, and the reverse held for a partner who shrank. Complementarity can feel like fit. But a fixed hierarchy is not the same as polarity. Simone de Beauvoir argued in The Second Sex (1949) that love becomes a trap when one person abandons their freedom to the other, and that authentic love would be two freedoms recognizing each other. Hegel's passage on lord and bondsman in the Phenomenology of Spirit (1807) suggests why: recognition from someone you have reduced to an instrument is worth nothing. The ancient Chinese image of yin and yang, each holding a seed of the other, describes the healthier dance. The charge stays alive when each partner can command and each can yield, and when surrender is a gift from strength rather than a tax paid by weakness.

tales.title: The Empress and the Would-Be Monk
tales.who: Catherine II of Russia and Grigory Potemkin
tales.where: St Petersburg and the southern steppe
tales.source: the surviving correspondence of Catherine and Potemkin; Simon Sebag Montefiore, Prince of Princes (2000)
tales.tale:
By 1774 Catherine the Great had ruled Russia for twelve years, having seized the throne in a coup against her own husband. She was forty-four, brilliant, tireless, and lonely in the way only autocrats are. Her current favourite was a handsome, dutiful guardsman whom she privately found dull.

Grigory Potemkin had been a young officer in the coup of 1762. He was ten years younger than she, huge, untidy, blind in one eye, a gambler and a mimic who could imitate her voice to her face and make her laugh. He was also learned, devout, moody and fearless. Early in 1774, back from the Turkish war at her invitation, he did something no courtier would dare: he withdrew to the Alexander Nevsky Monastery and let it be known he might take vows, since the one woman he wanted was out of reach. The empress, who could command anything, sent for him.

Their letters, hundreds of notes carried between their apartments, show a love that refused to sit still in its roles. She signs as a sovereign and writes like a girl. She calls him darling, my golden pheasant, my twin soul, and admits that her heart rules her. He sulks, storms out, makes demands, then writes tenderly. She scolds him like a schoolmistress and, a line later, begs him to come. Many historians believe they married in secret, probably in 1774; no record survives and it remains disputed.

The first fire cooled within about two years, but the polarity did not end; it changed shape. Potemkin stepped back as lover and became something rarer: her partner in power. She gave him the south, and he conquered and built it, annexing Crimea in 1783, founding cities and a Black Sea fleet. He contradicted her in council, and she deferred to him where she knew he understood more; he bowed to her as empress and spoke to her as an equal in private. Later favourites came, several of them, it seems, with his approval.

In October 1791, burning with fever on the road across the Bessarabian steppe, he asked to be lifted out of his carriage and died lying on the grass. In St Petersburg Catherine fainted at the news and wept for days. To her friend Baron Grimm she wrote that she had lost her pupil, her friend, almost her idol.
tales.reveals: Catherine held all the formal power, yet the bond came alive because Potemkin would not simply submit, and because she, the autocrat, chose to yield in private. Their partnership outlived passion because power kept moving between them instead of freezing into ruler and subject.

tales.title: Royalty Is a Good Burial Shroud
tales.who: Empress Theodora and Emperor Justinian I
tales.where: the Great Palace and the Hippodrome, Constantinople
tales.source: Procopius, History of the Wars I.24, and his hostile Secret History; the speech is Procopius's literary version
tales.tale:
Theodora began life in the Hippodrome. Her father kept bears for the Green faction; after his death her mother put her daughters on the stage. Procopius, who came to loathe her, later wrote a scabrous account of her youth as an actress and courtesan, and no one can say how much of it is slander. What is certain is that the heir to the throne, Justinian, a serious, sleepless man from the Balkans, wanted her so much that the law forbidding men of senatorial rank to marry actresses was changed. They married around 525, and when he became emperor in 527 she was crowned beside him, not behind him.

In January 532 the city exploded. The Blue and Green circus factions, usually at each other's throats, united against the emperor's ministers and their taxes. Their cry was “Nika!”, conquer, the shout used to cheer charioteers. For days they burned the city: the great church of Hagia Sophia, the Senate house, the bronze gate of the palace. Then the crowd crowned a nobleman, Hypatius, as emperor in the Hippodrome. Ships waited in the palace harbour, and Justinian's council debated whether to flee.

Then, Procopius says, Theodora spoke. It was not seemly, she granted, for a woman to speak among men, but this was no hour for propriety. Everyone born must die; but for one who has been an emperor, to become a fugitive is not to be borne. If flight is what you want, she told her husband, there is the sea and there are the ships. As for her, she approved an old saying: royalty is a good burial shroud.

The council rallied. The generals Belisarius and Mundus led their troops into the Hippodrome and trapped the crowd inside, and Procopius puts the dead at more than thirty thousand. Hypatius was executed the next day. Within weeks Justinian began rebuilding Hagia Sophia, the church that still stands.

Historians are rightly cautious. Procopius composed speeches in the manner of Thucydides, and Theodora's line adapts a saying attributed centuries earlier to Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse. But the shape of the marriage rings true. He held the throne; in the hour when he faltered, she held the line, and he was strong enough to let her.
tales.reveals: Justinian held the title, yet in the decisive hour he leaned on Theodora's steel, and the marriage drew strength from that exchange rather than shame. Power that can pass between partners in a crisis is a form of deep trust. The cost of that resolve, thousands dead in the Hippodrome, is a reminder that strength without mercy is nothing to admire.

practice: Notice who leads in your ordinary life together (plans, money, conversation, the bedroom) and deliberately swap roles for one evening.
Practise leading with warmth: plan a date in full, choose the place and the hour, and invite rather than asking permission for every detail.
Practise surrender as a strength: let her choose, follow wholeheartedly, and resist the urge to correct or take back the wheel.
Talk openly, outside the moment, about the kinds of leading and yielding you each enjoy, and what is off limits.
principles.shadow: Polarity turns toxic when one person is always in charge, when surrender is extracted rather than given, or when 'play' becomes cover for control. The dance only works if either partner can stop it, and if both leave it feeling larger.

principles.title: Court the one you already have
principles.motto: The first courtship wins a woman; every later one keeps her.
principles.essence: Most love stories stop at the wedding, as if the seduction were over. The deeper art is to keep courting the woman beside you: to see her freshly, write to her, surprise her, and choose her again long after the novelty has gone.
principles.depth: Psychologists call it hedonic adaptation: Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell (1971) proposed that we drift back to a baseline after almost any change, and lovers are no exception. Passionate love typically declines over the first years of a relationship. But the decline is not fate. Bianca Acevedo, Arthur Aron, Helen Fisher and Lucy Brown (2012) scanned the brains of people who reported still being intensely in love after an average of about twenty-one years of marriage, and found reward regions, including the ventral tegmental area, responding to the partner's face much as they do in new lovers, alongside activity linked to calm attachment. Aron's team (2000) found that couples who did novel, mildly exciting things together reported higher relationship quality afterwards, as if each new shared experience reopened the first. Philosophy has its own version. Søren Kierkegaard, in Repetition (1843), contrasted recollection, which looks backward and mourns, with repetition, which takes up the same love again moving forward and finds it new. Alain Badiou, in In Praise of Love (2009), argued that love is not the moment of encounter but a long construction, a life lived from the point of view of two. Renewal is that construction made tender: courtship as a practice, not a phase.

tales.title: Dearest Friend
tales.who: John and Abigail Adams
tales.where: Braintree (now Quincy), Massachusetts; Philadelphia; Paris; London
tales.source: the Adams Family Papers, Massachusetts Historical Society: over a thousand letters between John and Abigail
tales.tale:
In October 1762 a young lawyer named John Adams, twenty-six and rather pleased with himself, wrote a mock legal order to Miss Abigail Smith, a minister's daughter of seventeen who read more than anyone he knew. He addressed it to “Miss Adorable” and commanded her to give the bearer “as many Kisses, and as many Hours of your Company after 9 O'Clock as he shall please to Demand.” They married in 1764. It might have been the end of the courtship. It turned out to be the first of more than a thousand letters.

History kept pulling them apart. In 1774 John went to Philadelphia for the Continental Congress, and Abigail ran the farm at Braintree, raised four children, nursed the household through an epidemic of dysentery, and climbed a hill near home with her small son John Quincy to watch the smoke of the battle of Bunker Hill. She wrote to him as “Dearest Friend,” and he answered in kind. In March 1776, while he helped invent a nation, she told him to “remember the ladies” in the new code of laws, and to be more generous to them than their ancestors had been. He replied that he could not help laughing. She did not let it drop.

What makes the letters a love story is that they never settle into mere reports. They argue politics as equals. They tease, they ache, they flirt across months of silence. She protests when his letters grow short and businesslike; he confesses how much he misses home. In their early letters they wore names from the classics: she was Diana, later Portia, and he was Lysander.

In 1778 John sailed for Europe as a diplomat. After a brief return in 1779 he sailed again, and they did not see each other for nearly five years. In December 1782 Abigail wrote that she recollected “the untitled Man to whom I gave my Heart,” and in the agony of time and distance wished he had never been any other. In 1784 she crossed the Atlantic herself, and they were reunited in London.

They were married for fifty-four years. When Abigail died of typhoid fever in October 1818, John, now eighty-three, is reported to have said that he wished he could lie down beside her and die too.
tales.reveals: The Adamses kept courting each other on paper for decades, through war, separation, illness and fame, and their letters never stopped being addressed to a person rather than a spouse. Renewal is not a grand gesture but the steady habit of telling the other what they still mean, in words that could only be for them.

tales.title: The Oak and the Linden
tales.who: Baucis and Philemon, with Jupiter and Mercury
tales.when: myth (Ovid wrote it down c. AD 8)
tales.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses VIII, told by Lelex at the house of the river god Achelous
tales.tale:
Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as weary travellers, came down into the hills of Phrygia and knocked at a thousand doors in search of rest. A thousand doors were bolted against them. Only one opened: a small hut thatched with straw and marsh reeds, where Baucis and Philemon had married young and grown old together, making their poverty light by admitting it and bearing it with good temper.

The visitors stooped under the low lintel. Philemon set out a bench, and Baucis threw a rough cloth over it. She raked the warm ashes, fed them dry leaves and bark, and coaxed them into flame with her old breath. He had gathered greens from the garden, and she stripped the leaves from a cabbage. With a forked stick he lifted down a side of smoked bacon that had hung from the blackened beam for a long time and cut a small piece of the treasure to boil.

The table had one short leg, and Baucis wedged it level with a shard of broken pot, then scrubbed the top with green mint. She served olives, cornel cherries pickled in wine lees, endive, radish, cheese and eggs turned lightly in the ashes, all in earthenware, with cups of beechwood lined with yellow wax. For dessert there were nuts, figs, dates, plums, apples, grapes and a white honeycomb. Above all, Ovid says, there were kindly faces.

Then they noticed the wine bowl kept filling itself. Terrified, they tried to catch their only goose to kill it for the gods, and the goose fled to the guests for protection. The gods forbade the sacrifice, revealed themselves, and led the old couple up the mountain. Behind them the whole valley drowned in marsh; their hut alone became a marble temple.

Asked for a wish, they conferred and asked only to be its priests and, since they had lived in harmony so long, to die in the same hour, so that neither would see the other's grave. Years later, standing before the temple steps, each saw the other begin to put out leaves. While they still could, they spoke, and said farewell together as the bark closed over their lips. Lelex swore he had seen the two trees himself, an oak and a linden, hung with fresh garlands.
tales.reveals: Baucis and Philemon never stopped serving each other and their guests with care, and their tenderness after a lifetime is exactly what the gods reward. Renewal here is humble and daily: fanning the fire, levelling the table, setting out the best you have. A long love becomes sacred not through drama but through attention that never goes stale.

practice: Write her a real note this week, by hand, about something you have noticed in her recently, not something from the early days.
Plan a date as if you still had to win her: dress for it, book it, and arrive with a question you genuinely want answered.
Do one new thing together that slightly unsettles you both: a class, an unfamiliar neighbourhood, a night swim.
Each evening before sleep, name aloud one thing she did that day that you liked.
principles.shadow: Renewal curdles into performance when it becomes a show for others or a way of papering over problems you refuse to discuss. Courtship cannot replace honesty; it only works on top of it.

principles.title: When love is refused, transform it
principles.motto: What you cannot hold, you can still make immortal.
principles.essence: Not every desire will be answered, and some should not be. When love is refused or impossible, you are not obliged to rot in it or to force it: you can turn its heat into work, art and a larger self. The person who transmutes longing becomes more magnetic, not less.
principles.depth: Freud used the word sublimation in Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905) for the redirection of erotic energy toward cultural aims, and in Civilization and Its Discontents (1930) he made it one of the engines of art and science. You need not accept his hydraulic model to see the truth in it. Roy Baumeister, Sara Wotman and Arlene Stillwell (1993) collected accounts of unrequited love and found that the rejected lover often suffers from what they called “scriptlessness”: no social script tells them what to do with the feeling. Sublimation is a script. James Pennebaker's experiments on expressive writing (Pennebaker and Beall, 1986) showed that putting painful emotion into structured words improved health and mood over the following months, though later meta-analyses find the effect real but modest. The older map is Plato's: in the Symposium, Diotima describes a ladder on which love of one beautiful body rises to love of beautiful souls, of laws, of knowledge, and finally of beauty itself. The troubadours and the poets of the dolce stil novo knew the same alchemy. The point is not to deny desire but to give it a direction where no door is open, so that refusal makes you larger instead of bitter.

tales.title: The Girl in Crimson
tales.who: Dante Alighieri and Beatrice (traditionally identified as Bice Portinari)
tales.source: Dante, Vita Nuova (c. 1294) and Divine Comedy, Purgatorio XXX; the identification of Beatrice comes from Boccaccio
tales.tale:
Florence, 1274, a spring feast at the house of Folco Portinari. A boy of nine, Dante Alighieri, sees a girl of about eight dressed in a subdued, noble crimson, girdled and adorned as befits her age. Years later he wrote that at that instant the spirit of life, trembling in the most secret chamber of his heart, spoke: “Here is a god stronger than I, who comes to rule over me.” Whether a child truly felt this, or the poet shaped the memory into a myth, nobody can know. What is certain is what he did with it.

Nine years passed. Then, on a Florentine street, she appeared again, now dressed in purest white, walking between two older ladies. She turned her eyes toward the place where he stood, frozen, and greeted him. That greeting, a few words and a nod, sent him home in a fever. He shut himself in his room, fell asleep, and dreamed of a lordly figure holding a sleeping woman wrapped in a crimson cloth and feeding her his burning heart.

That was nearly the whole of their acquaintance. To hide his feeling he pretended to love other women, his “screen ladies,” and the gossip grew so loud that Beatrice withheld her greeting altogether. He was devastated, and here the turn begins. When a circle of women asked him what the point was of a love that received nothing, he answered that his happiness now lay in words that praise her. He stopped waiting for her favour and started writing.

Beatrice married the banker Simone de' Bardi. She died on 8 June 1290, aged twenty four. Dante gathered his poems and prose into the Vita Nuova and closed it with a vow: he would say nothing more of her until he could say of her what had never been said of any woman.

He kept the vow. Exiled from Florence in 1302, poor and wandering from court to court, he built the Divine Comedy, a hundred cantos in which Beatrice is the one who sends Virgil to rescue him from the dark wood. At the summit of Purgatory she arrives veiled and crowned with olive, and before he even sees her face he trembles: “I recognize the signs of the ancient flame,” a line borrowed from Virgil's Dido. Then she scolds him, sharply, for wasting his gifts after her death. A refused love had become a guide.
tales.reveals: Dante's love had almost nothing to feed on: two meetings, a greeting, a loss. Because he could not possess Beatrice, he made her the axis of his whole art, and a longing that could have soured into resentment became one of the summits of world literature.

tales.title: The Laurel and the Breeze
tales.who: Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch) and Laura
tales.source: Petrarch, Canzoniere (Rerum vulgarium fragmenta); his note on the flyleaf of the Ambrosian Virgil; his letter on the ascent of Mont Ventoux (Familiares IV.1). Laura's identity is disputed.
tales.tale:
On 6 April 1327, a day he remembered as Good Friday, in the church of Saint Clare at Avignon, a twenty two year old Italian cleric named Francesco Petrarca saw a woman with golden hair and felt himself undone. He calls her Laura. Who she was remains disputed: the favourite candidate is Laura de Noves, wife of Hugues de Sade and mother of many children. Even in his lifetime friends teased him that she was an invention, and Petrarch protested, with some heat, that she was real.

She was beyond his reach in every way: married, virtuous, and he a man in minor orders. As far as the poems tell it, she gave him little more than a glance, a greeting, now and then a cool look he read as reproach. So he did something strange. He turned her name into a pun that could hold the world. Laura became l'aura, the breeze, and lauro, the laurel, Apollo's tree and the crown of poets. Whenever the wind moved in the leaves near his retreat at Vaucluse, by the cold green source of the Sorgue, she was there.

In April 1336, by his own account, he climbed Mont Ventoux with his brother Gherardo. At the summit, looking toward Italy, he opened the pocket copy of Augustine's Confessions he carried and read a passage rebuking men who admire mountains and oceans and neglect their own souls. He walked down in silence. Scholars doubt the climb happened quite as he tells it, but the letter shows his project: to turn outward longing inward.

On 8 April 1341, on the Capitoline Hill in Rome, he was crowned with laurel as a poet. Laura's tree rested on his head.

Then came the Black Death. On a flyleaf of his treasured Virgil he wrote that Laura had died in Avignon on 6 April 1348, the same day of the same month on which he had first seen her, at the first hour of the morning. He added that he wrote the note where his eyes would often fall on it, so that he would remember nothing was left to hold him in this life.

He did not stop. For the rest of his life he polished the poems, ordering them into 366 pieces, songs of her life and songs of her death. Those sonnets taught Europe how to speak of love for three centuries.
tales.reveals: Petrarch's desire had no future, so he gave it form, and form gave him a vocation. Sublimation is not the absence of longing: it is longing given a discipline, a craft and a direction.

practice: If someone you want has said no, or is not free, say it plainly to yourself once: “This will not happen.” Then choose one thing to build with that energy this week: a piece of writing, a training plan, a skill you have postponed.
Write a letter you will never send, describing what this person awakened in you rather than what you wanted from her. Keep what it teaches you about your own taste.
Name the qualities you admired in her (courage, wit, ease) and practise one of them yourself, in public, this week.
Mute or unfollow her for a while if watching her life keeps the wound open. Distance is not defeat; it is how the energy gets redirected.
principles.shadow: Sublimation curdles when it becomes a secret siege: the devoted friend who is really waiting for a chance, or the artist who turns a real person into a public obsession. Transform the feeling for your own growth, never at the cost of her peace or privacy.

principles.title: Know the dark arts, refuse them
principles.motto: Learn every trick, so you never need one and never fall for one.
principles.essence: Every technique of influence can be bent into manipulation: false scarcity, staged jealousy, the hot and cold game. Know these moves well enough to recognize them, in others and in yourself, and then decline to use them. Real allure is a power that leaves the other person freer than it found her.
principles.depth: Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams (2002) named the Dark Triad: narcissism, Machiavellianism and psychopathy. Richard Christie and Florence Geis (1970) had already measured Machiavellianism with their Mach IV scale and found high scorers cool, strategic and often effective in short, competitive encounters. Peter Jonason and colleagues (2009) reported that dark traits correlate with more short-term partners, a finding much quoted by pickup gurus and less often quoted with its sequel: the same traits predict lower relationship satisfaction, more infidelity and shorter commitments. Manipulation works, briefly. Its cost is that it destroys the very thing it imitates, which is trust. Kant drew the clearest line in the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785): treat humanity, in yourself and in others, never merely as a means but always also as an end. Seduction that respects that line invites; manipulation engineers. Laclos understood this in 1782. His novel is a manual of tactics written to make you sick of tactics: every letter brilliant, every victory hollow, both masterminds destroyed by the machine they run. To know the dark arts is protection. To use them is to become someone no one can trust, including yourself.

tales.title: Two Generals of the Bedroom
tales.who: The Marquise de Merteuil and the Vicomte de Valmont
tales.where: Paris and the country house of Madame de Rosemonde
tales.source: Pierre Choderlos de Laclos, Les Liaisons dangereuses (1782), an epistolary novel; fiction
tales.tale:
Pierre Choderlos de Laclos was an artillery officer stuck in dull garrison towns when he wrote a novel in letters that set Paris talking in 1782. Its two heroes are former lovers who now treat seduction as a sport, writing to each other like generals comparing maps.

The Marquise de Merteuil, a widow with a spotless reputation, wants revenge on a man who once left her. She asks the Vicomte de Valmont to corrupt Cécile de Volanges, a fifteen year old fresh from the convent who is engaged to that very man. Valmont finds the task beneath him. He has a grander target: Madame de Tourvel, a devout and faithful wife staying at his aunt's country house. He wants her to fall not through weakness but against her own conscience, and to know, every step of the way, that she is falling.

Merteuil explains herself in the famous letter eighty one. As a girl, she writes, she studied her own face in secret, learning to look serene while she was in pain and to show joy she did not feel. She taught herself to observe and to hide. She had been born, she declares, to avenge her sex and to master yours. It is a dazzling self-portrait and a chilling one: a woman who has turned herself into an instrument.

Valmont pursues Tourvel with staged charity to a poor family, intercepted letters and well-timed tears. She resists for months, then gives way. And something happens that he did not plan: he is happy with her. Merteuil sees it and mocks him for being in love. To prove he is still free, Valmont copies out a letter she has drafted and sends it to Tourvel. Each paragraph ends with the same shrug: “It is not my fault.”

The lines destroy her. Tourvel withdraws to a convent, falls into fever and dies. Valmont is killed in a duel by Cécile's young admirer, the Chevalier Danceny, and before dying hands over Merteuil's letters. Paris reads them. At the theatre the audience hisses her in her box. Smallpox ravages her face, and a character remarks that her soul is now visible on it. She loses her lawsuit and flees, alone, to Holland.

The game had worked perfectly. That was the catastrophe.
tales.reveals: Laclos shows that mastery of manipulation is a trap for the master. Valmont's one moment of real feeling is the single thing the game cannot allow, and killing it to keep his reputation as a player costs him everything.

tales.title: The Spanish Dancer from Sligo
tales.who: Lola Montez (Eliza Gilbert) and King Ludwig I of Bavaria
tales.source: Contemporary accounts and Bruce Seymour, Lola Montez: A Life (1996); the bodice anecdote is legend
tales.tale:
She was born Eliza Gilbert in County Sligo, Ireland, in 1821, the daughter of a British army officer, and spent part of her childhood in India. After an elopement and a failed marriage she reinvented herself in London in 1843 as Lola Montez, a Spanish dancer of noble Sevillian blood. Someone in the audience at her debut recognized her as Mrs James almost at once. She simply crossed to the Continent and kept the name.

In October 1846 she arrived in Munich and asked to dance at the court theatre. King Ludwig I of Bavaria, sixty years old, a passionate lover of art and of all things Spanish, received her. As the story is told, he wondered aloud whether her figure was entirely nature's work, and she took a pair of scissors from his desk and cut open her bodice to answer him. The anecdote is almost certainly embroidered, but it captures what Munich believed: she gave the king nerve, theatre and shock in place of court ritual.

Ludwig was enchanted. He wrote her poems by the dozen, took Spanish lessons from her, bought her a house, and in August 1847 made her Countess of Landsfeld. She meddled in appointments, quarrelled with ministers, swept through the streets with her big dog and made scenes with anyone who crossed her. The persona had worked so well that she began to believe it had no limit.

It did. Catholic conservatives hated her, liberals resented her, and in February 1848 students rioted after she surrounded herself with a fraternity of young admirers loyal only to her. The crowd stoned her house. Ludwig signed the order expelling her. A month later, with revolution sweeping Europe, he abdicated in favour of his son Maximilian. How physical their affair ever was remains debated; what is certain is that it cost him his crown.

Lola went on to New York, the California gold country and Australia, performing her own legend on stage. She died in New York in January 1861, aged thirty nine, poor, after a stroke, having spent her last months visiting outcast women and lecturing on beauty and morals.

It is fair to add that much of what was written about her came from enemies, and was coloured by contempt for any woman who wielded power. But her method was a mask, and a mask has to be fed every single day.
tales.reveals: Lola's invented self opened a palace door, but a persona built to manage a man has to be managed forever, and sooner or later it collides with reality. The lesson is not that boldness fails; it is that a false identity turns every intimacy into a performance and every ally into an audience that will one day walk out.

practice: Make a private list of the tactics you know: playing hard to get on a schedule, invented rivals, intermittent warmth, flattery with an agenda. This week, notice each time you feel tempted toward one and name it silently.
Replace one tactic with its honest twin: instead of pretending to be busy, say “I'd love to, but not tonight. Thursday?” Notice that a real limit carries the same charge as a fake one.
When someone uses a move on you (guilt, sudden coldness, a flood of flattery), name it out loud, kindly: “It feels like I'm being tested. I'd rather you just tell me.”
Before you send a flirtatious message, ask: would I be comfortable if she could read my reasons for sending it? If not, rewrite it.
principles.shadow: The danger is the clever reader who studies manipulation for protection and slowly starts using it. The line is simple: any technique that only works if the other person cannot see it is out.

principles.title: The conqueror's hunger
principles.motto: Collect conquests and you will starve at a feast.
principles.essence: Seduction kept as a scorecard leaves you hungrier with every win. The conqueror chases the moment of yielding, and that moment is always already over. Recognize this hunger in yourself, and choose depth over number.
principles.depth: Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell (1971) called it the hedonic treadmill: we adapt to gains and drift back to baseline, so the next gain must be bigger. Brickman, Coates and Janoff-Bulman (1978) found lottery winners no happier than controls some time later; the study was small, and later work shows adaptation is not always complete, but the pattern holds well enough to worry any collector. Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson (1998) separated wanting from liking in the brain's reward systems: dopamine drives the craving for a reward far more than the pleasure of having it, which is why a pursuit can feel urgent and its success strangely flat. Philosophy got there first. Schopenhauer, in The World as Will and Representation (1818), described life swinging like a pendulum between the pain of wanting and the boredom of having. Kierkegaard in Either/Or (1843) made Don Juan the emblem of the aesthetic life, a string of moments that never adds up to a self. Pascal saw our endless diversions as a way to avoid sitting quietly alone in a room. The conqueror is not too full of desire; he is too empty to hold any.

tales.title: Supper with the Stone Guest
tales.who: Don Juan Tenorio and the statue of the Commander Don Gonzalo de Ulloa
tales.when: c. 1630 (play), set in the fourteenth century
tales.where: Naples, the coast of Tarragona and Seville
tales.source: El burlador de Sevilla y convidado de piedra, attributed to Tirso de Molina (published c. 1630); later retold by Molière (Dom Juan, 1665) and by Mozart and Da Ponte (Don Giovanni, 1787). Fiction.
tales.tale:
The play opens in darkness, in the royal palace of Naples. The Duchess Isabela has welcomed a man she believes is her betrothed, Duke Octavio. She calls for a light. When she demands to know who he is, he answers that he is a man without a name. He is Don Juan Tenorio, a young nobleman of Seville, and he escapes before the guards can hold him.

That is his whole art: disguise, promise, flight. Shipwrecked on the coast of Tarragona, he is pulled from the sea by Tisbea, a fisherwoman proud of never having loved. He swears to marry her, enjoys her, and rides away on her own mares, leaving her crying “Fire!” on the shore, as if her hut and her heart had caught at once. In Seville he slips into the room of Doña Ana de Ulloa wrapped in another man's cloak. Her father, the Commander Don Gonzalo, rushes in with his sword. Don Juan kills him. Then he crashes a peasant wedding and persuades the bride, Aminta, that a lord's promise outranks a farmer's vow.

Whenever anyone warns him that God's judgment will come, Don Juan has one careless reply: “¡Qué largo me lo fiáis!” Roughly: what a long credit you give me. Death is far off; repentance can wait.

One night he passes the Commander's tomb and reads the inscription promising vengeance on the traitor who killed him. He laughs, mocks the stone beard, and invites the statue to supper. At his house there is a knock. The statue enters, sits, and invites him in return to dine in its chapel. Don Juan, too proud to look afraid, goes.

The table there is draped in black. The dishes are scorpions and vipers, the wine is gall and vinegar, and the singers chant that there is no deadline that does not arrive and no debt that is not paid. When the meal is done the statue asks for his hand. Don Juan gives it and cries out that he is burning. He begs for a priest, for a chance to confess. Too late: the credit has run out, and the stone drags him down into the grave.

It is a religious play, built to frighten an audience. But beneath the sermon lies a portrait: a man who can begin everything and finish nothing, whose only proof that he exists is the next woman.
tales.reveals: Don Juan cannot stay anywhere, because staying would mean being known. His conquests are not appetite satisfied but appetite outrunning itself, and the stone hand is the bill for a life made only of beginnings.

tales.title: The Librarian of Dux
tales.who: Giacomo Casanova and the household of Count Waldstein
tales.source: Casanova, Histoire de ma vie and his letters and complaints written at Dux; the recollections of the Prince de Ligne; biographies such as Ian Kelly, Casanova (2008)
tales.tale:
In 1785 the most famous lover in Europe was sixty, nearly penniless, exiled from Venice for the second time, and grateful for a job. Count Joseph Karl von Waldstein, a young aristocrat who had enjoyed his conversation, offered him the post of librarian at his castle of Dux in northern Bohemia: a salary, rooms, and a collection usually put at around forty thousand books.

The count was often away. Casanova was left among servants who found the old Venetian absurd: his powdered wig and out-of-date velvet, his elaborate bows, his complaints that the macaroni was badly made, his German that nobody understood and his French that nobody cared about. The steward Feldkirchner and the courier Wiederholt made a sport of tormenting him. According to Casanova's own furious complaints, someone tore his portrait out of one of his books, smeared it with filth and nailed it up in the privy. He wrote long letters of protest. The servants went on laughing.

Visitors such as the Prince de Ligne found him brilliant and exhausting, quick to take offence at any sign of disrespect, eager to read aloud from his own works.

In this exile he began, around 1789, to write the story of his life in French. He told a correspondent that he wrote thirteen hours a day and that the hours passed like thirteen minutes, and he said that writing was what kept him from going mad. Page after page he returned to Henriette in Parma, to the nun M.M. in Venice, to the dozens of women whose names, or false names, he had kept. He relived the chase in ink because he could no longer live it in the flesh.

The memoir is one of the great documents of the eighteenth century, frank, funny, often generous to the women in it. It is also, read in the light of Dux, a long hunger. The man who had collected so many beginnings found at the end that he had no home of his own, no wife, no family around him, and a library that belonged to someone else.

He died at Dux on 4 June 1798. Legend gives him a fine last line about having lived as a philosopher and dying as a Christian; it may be true, or one more of his stories. The manuscript, thousands of pages long, was not published in full until the 1960s.
tales.reveals: Casanova's Dux years show the bill the conqueror finally pays: when the pursuit ends, the conquests do not add up to a life that holds you. Even his genius could only turn the hunger into memory, replayed night after night at a borrowed desk.

practice: Be honest on paper: in your romantic life, how much energy goes into winning attention, and how much into what comes after? Write both down as rough percentages.
This week, when you feel the itch to check whether someone new still wants you (a message, a like, a glance), wait an hour and ask what you are actually hungry for.
Choose one existing connection, romantic or not, and deepen it: ask a question you have never asked them, and stay for the long answer.
Spend thirty minutes alone without your phone or company. Notice what rises when there is no one to impress. That restlessness is the conqueror's hunger; befriend it instead of feeding it.
principles.shadow: Seeing the hunger clearly can tip into self-contempt, or into a cynical belief that all desire is empty. The point is not to stop desiring but to stop using people as proof of your worth.

principles.title: Grace, consent and the reading of signs
principles.motto: The finest seducer listens hardest for the word no.
principles.essence: Courtesy is the art of making desire safe to express and safe to refuse. Read signals with care, ask when you are unsure, and accept a no with such grace that the other person feels freer, not smaller. Nothing is more attractive than interest that never turns into pressure.
principles.depth: Erving Goffman's essay On Face-Work (1955) and Penelope Brown and Stephen Levinson's Politeness (1987) describe courtesy as the protection of face: our wish to be approved of and our wish not to be imposed upon. Flirtation is a delicate negotiation of both at once. Research on sexual consent, reviewed by Charlene Muehlenhard and colleagues (2016), finds that people rely heavily on indirect, nonverbal cues, and that these cues are often misread; since Antonia Abbey's study (1982), many experiments have found men overestimating women's sexual interest in friendly behaviour. The lesson is not to abandon nuance but to check it: a light, direct question costs nothing and builds trust. Medieval culture made courtesy a discipline. The word itself comes from the court, and the troubadours' ideal of fin'amor demanded patience, humility and service to a lady who held the power to grant or to refuse. Simone Weil wrote to Joë Bousquet in 1942 that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. Courtesy is attention turned into manners: noticing hesitation, offering an easy exit, and letting a yes be given freely, which is the only kind of yes worth having.

tales.title: The Judgments of Love
tales.who: Eleanor of Aquitaine, Marie de Champagne and Andreas Capellanus
tales.source: Andreas Capellanus, De amore (On Love), c. 1186 to 1190; historians such as John F. Benton argue the courts of love never sat as real tribunals
tales.tale:
In the 1170s, as the story goes, the great hall at Poitiers became a courtroom where every case was a matter of the heart. Eleanor of Aquitaine, once queen of France and now the estranged queen of England, presided with her daughter Marie, Countess of Champagne, among ladies who heard lovers' disputes and handed down verdicts. Her grandfather, Duke William IX, is the first troubadour whose songs survive, and in these rooms young knights were expected to learn not only to fight but to speak, to wait and to serve.

Our main witness is a cleric of Marie's court at Troyes, Andreas, called the Chaplain, who wrote a Latin treatise on love around 1186 to 1190. He records judgments with names and even dates. In one, presented as a letter from Countess Marie dated 1 May 1174, the question is whether true love can exist between husband and wife. She rules that it cannot, because spouses give by duty what lovers must give freely. In another, a lover who had betrayed his lady's secrets is judged unworthy of any lady's love thereafter.

The liveliest pages are dialogues. A man of the middle class addresses a noblewoman; a nobleman addresses a lady of higher rank. Each pleads, flatters and argues, and in case after case the lady answers with wit and holds her ground. She may grant hope, postpone, or refuse outright; the man must accept her answer and argue better, not seize what she withholds. In this world love is a gift, never a tax.

Did the courts really sit? Probably not as formal tribunals. The historian John Benton argued that they are largely a literary fiction, and Andreas is often playful, even ironic: his third book abruptly condemns love altogether. The code also had an ugly limit. In one short chapter Andreas tells a nobleman that if he desires a peasant woman he need not bother courting her, and may use a little force. Courtesy, for him, stopped at the border of class.

Yet the ideal outlived its hypocrisies. Here, in a churchman's Latin, a woman's freedom to choose was set at the centre of the game, and the lover's task was to deserve a yes rather than to take one.
tales.reveals: Whether real or imagined, the courts of love made a woman's yes precious precisely because her no was respected. And Andreas's chapter on peasants shows exactly where any code of courtesy fails: the moment it decides that some people's refusals do not count.

tales.title: Three Mornings at Hautdesert
tales.who: Sir Gawain and the lady of Hautdesert (Lady Bertilak)
tales.where: the castle of Hautdesert, somewhere beyond the Wirral in north-west England
tales.source: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, anonymous Middle English poem (British Library, Cotton Nero A.x); fiction
tales.tale:
Christmas is ending, and Sir Gawain must soon go to his death. A year ago at Camelot he struck off the head of a green giant who then picked it up and rode away, and Gawain promised to seek him out and receive a blow in return. Lost in the frozen forests, he finds a shining castle, a jovial lord named Bertilak, and a lady lovelier, the poet says, than Guinevere herself.

The lord proposes a game. Each day he will hunt while Gawain rests, and each evening they will exchange whatever they have won.

On the first morning Gawain hears the door creak softly. He pretends to sleep, peeking through the bed curtains. The lady sits on the edge of his bed and teases him: the famous knight, caught napping, is now her prisoner. She is bold, and she says it plainly, in the poem's own words: “Ye ar welcum to my cors,” you are welcome to my body. Scholars still debate how to read the line, but its invitation is unmistakable.

Gawain's position is delicate. She is his host's wife; he is a guest bound by loyalty and by his own vows. Yet he is also famous for courtesy, and she uses that: surely so courteous a knight cannot refuse a lady anything? He answers with humour and humility, protesting that he is unworthy of her praise, turning each advance into a compliment without accepting it. He grants a single kiss. That evening, gravely, he kisses the lord once in exchange for a heap of venison.

The second morning, two kisses for a boar. The third, three kisses for a fox, and the lady pressing harder, asking whether he loves another. He tells her no, and that he will take no lover now. She offers a gold ring, which he refuses, then her green silk girdle, which she swears will keep its wearer from being killed. This he takes, and hides. That night he gives the lord three kisses, and keeps the girdle back.

At the Green Chapel the axe falls three times: a flinch, a feint, and a nick on the neck. The Green Knight reveals that he is Bertilak; the mornings were a test, and the nick was the price of the hidden girdle. Gawain, ashamed, wears the green band ever after. At Camelot the court laughs kindly and adopts it as a sash of honour.
tales.reveals: Gawain shows how to decline without humiliating: warmth, wit and a firm boundary, so that the lady's dignity is never at stake. His one failure, hiding the girdle, is a failure of honesty rather than of desire, and the poem treats his confession as the beginning of a deeper courtesy.

practice: Ask one clear question this week where you would usually guess: “Would you like to stay for another drink?” or “Can I kiss you?” Say it warmly, as an invitation, not as an anxious request.
Practise the graceful no: when you decline someone's advance, add something true and kind, as Gawain did, so they leave with their dignity intact.
Watch for signs of hesitation (a pause, a glance at the door, shorter answers) and offer an easy exit: “No pressure at all, we can call it a night here.”
When a woman turns you down, answer lightly and mean it: “Thank you for telling me.” Then change the subject, and let her see that nothing between you has been lost.
principles.shadow: Courtesy can harden into performance: elaborate manners used to corner someone, or a show of respect that sulks after a refusal. If your politeness makes it harder to say no to you, it is not courtesy.

principles.title: Become the one worth desiring
principles.motto: Do not chase her desire. Become a life worth joining.
principles.essence: Every technique in this book is surface unless there is substance underneath. The deepest allure comes from who you are becoming: your loyalties, your work, your courage, the depth of your attention. Choose meaning over mere pleasure, and you become someone others want to walk beside.
principles.depth: David Buss's survey of mate preferences across 37 cultures (1989) found that kindness and intelligence ranked at or near the top for both sexes, above looks and wealth, though the same study reported sex differences in emphasis that are still debated. Character, in other words, is not a consolation prize; it is what people say they want most. Arthur and Elaine Aron's self-expansion model suggests why: we are drawn to people whose inner world can enlarge our own. Aristotle anticipated both in the Nicomachean Ethics, books VIII and IX: friendships of pleasure and of use dissolve when the pleasure or the use runs out, while friendships of virtue last, because each person loves the other for what they are. Erich Fromm, in The Art of Loving (1956), argued that most people treat love as a problem of being lovable, when it is really a capacity: the ability to love. The Sufi readers of Layla and Majnun added a last turn, in which the beloved becomes a mirror for something greater than both lovers. Worth is not a pose to project. It is a practice of becoming, and attraction is its byproduct.

tales.title: The Raft on Ogygia
tales.who: Odysseus and the nymph Calypso
tales.source: Homer, Odyssey V
tales.tale:
For seven years Odysseus has lived on Ogygia, the island at the navel of the sea, with the nymph Calypso. Her cave is warm with a fire of cedar and fragrant citron wood. Around it grow alder, poplar and sweet-smelling cypress, where long-winged birds nest; a vine heavy with grapes climbs over the entrance; four springs run clear through meadows of violets and wild celery. Homer says that even a god, arriving there, would stand and marvel. Hermes, the messenger, does.

He brings an order from Zeus: let the man go. Calypso is furious. The gods, she says, are jealous whenever a goddess openly takes a mortal as her mate. She saved this one when Zeus's thunderbolt shattered his ship; she fed him, loved him, and promised to make him immortal and ageless forever. But she obeys.

She finds Odysseus where he spends his days: sitting on the shore, looking out over the barren sea, weeping. Homer is precise about it. At night he sleeps beside her in the hollow cave, unwilling beside the willing. By day the sweetness of his life drains away in longing for home.

Calypso tells him he may build a raft. He suspects a trick and makes her swear a great oath that she means him no harm. Then, at their last supper, she tries once more. If you knew, she says, how many sorrows wait for you before you reach your own country, you would stay here with me and be immortal. And surely I am not less than your wife in form or stature; mortal women cannot rival goddesses.

His answer is a masterpiece of courtesy and resolve. Queen and goddess, he says, do not be angry with me. I know that wise Penelope is less than you to look upon, for she is mortal and you are ageless and deathless. Even so, I wish and long every day to reach my home and see the day of my return. And if some god wrecks me again on the wine-dark sea, I will endure it, for I have a heart that knows how to endure.

For four days he fells trees and builds the raft. On the fifth she bathes him, dresses him in fragrant clothes, loads wine, water and bread, and sends a gentle, warm wind. He sets his course by the Pleiades and the Bear, and he does not turn back.
tales.reveals: Odysseus turns down immortality because it would cost him the self he has built: a husband, a father, a man with a home to restore. His fidelity to his own life is what makes him worth desiring, even to a goddess. Worth means knowing what your life is for, and refusing to trade it for comfort, however beautiful.

tales.title: The Madman of Love
tales.who: Qays ibn al-Mulawwah, called Majnun, and Layla
tales.when: 1188 (Nizami's poem); the legend is older, set in seventh century Arabia
tales.source: Nizami Ganjavi, Layla and Majnun (1188), drawing on older Arabic legends; whether Qays was a real poet is disputed
tales.tale:
The story was old when Nizami of Ganja took it up in 1188, at the request of the Shirvanshah Akhsitan. Arab storytellers had long told of Qays, a young poet of the Banu Amir in Najd, who loved a girl named Layla. Nizami at first hesitated, he tells us, to set so bleak a desert tale, without gardens or feasts; then he made it a Persian masterpiece.

In his telling, the two meet as children at school and fall in love over their lessons. Their glances become poems, and Qays cannot keep the poems to himself: he recites them in the camps and lanes until the whole tribe knows Layla's name. That is the first wound. In their world a love sung in public shames a girl's family. Layla's father refuses the marriage, and people begin to call Qays majnun: the possessed, the mad one.

His father, desperate, takes him on pilgrimage to the Kaaba at Mecca and tells him to pray to be cured. Qays grips the ring of the sacred door and prays instead that his love may grow, that he may go on loving even if it destroys him. His father gives up.

Majnun goes into the desert. He lives among wild creatures, who gather around him like a court. When he finds a hunter with a gazelle in his snare, he trades what he has to set it free, because its dark eyes are Layla's eyes. Layla, meanwhile, is married against her will to a nobleman, Ibn Salam, but in Nizami she keeps herself from him and goes on sending word to Majnun in secret.

Once, in Nizami's poem, an old go-between brings them within sight of each other in a palm grove. Layla stops some ten paces away and will come no closer. Majnun recites verses to her, then runs back into the wilderness. Their love has passed beyond touch.

When her husband dies and Layla is free at last, it is too late; grief consumes her, and she dies in autumn. Majnun comes to her grave, lays his head upon it and dies there, and the animals keep watch over his body.

Sufi poets read the story as a parable of the soul's love for God. Nizami leaves the ambiguity standing: Majnun becomes a great poet and a holy fool, and loses the woman he became great for.
tales.reveals: Majnun's devotion made him a poet the whole East remembers, but it also consumed the life the lovers might have shared. Read beside Odysseus, he shows the two edges of worth: a love that refines who you are is magnificent, while a love that dissolves who you are leaves no one for the beloved to meet.

practice: Write down three things you would keep doing even if no one ever found you attractive: work, a craft, a cause, a friendship. Give one of them an extra hour this week.
Keep one small promise to yourself and one to someone else, both on time. Reliability is the quietest form of allure.
Learn something real you can share (a recipe, a poem by heart, how to find the Pleiades) and offer it the next time a conversation turns personal.
Ask yourself, as Odysseus might: what would I refuse, even if it were offered beautifully? Knowing your answer gives you a spine that others can feel.
principles.shadow: Self-improvement turns sour when it becomes one more strategy, polishing yourself only to be chosen, or a pedestal from which you judge others unworthy. Become worthy for the sake of the life itself, and let attraction follow as a side effect.
